cards.title: Linear probe
cards.what: Train a tiny linear model on hidden activations to test if some information is inside them.
cards.why: You cannot read activations by eye. You need a test that says 'yes, this layer knows the word is a verb'.
cards.how: Save the activations for many inputs. Fit logistic regression from activations to the label. Compare accuracy across layers.
cards.when: When you ask what a layer knows.
cards.extra: Like logistic regression, but the inputs are a network's hidden numbers.

cards.title: Probe accuracy trap
cards.what: A probe that scores high does not prove the model uses that information.
cards.why: People claimed 'the model uses X' from probe scores alone. That was often wrong.
cards.how: Compare against a control task, or follow up with a causal test such as activation patching.
cards.when: Before you trust any probe result.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.what: A network stores more ideas than it has neurons, by packing them at almost-right angles.
cards.why: Single neurons are confusing. One neuron fires for cats, cars and French text.
cards.how: Each feature is a direction. Sparse features rarely fire together, so their directions can overlap a little.
cards.when: Any time you look inside a model.
cards.extra: Like PCA, but with more directions than dimensions: $k > d$.

cards.title: Polysemantic neuron
cards.what: One neuron takes part in many unrelated ideas.
cards.why: It explains why 'what does neuron 42 do?' has no clean answer.
cards.when: When a neuron's top examples look random.
cards.extra: Opposite: a monosemantic neuron, which means one thing.

cards.title: Sparse autoencoder
cards.what: A small network that pulls the packed ideas apart, so each unit means one thing.
cards.why: Superposition hides features. We need a tool to un-mix them.
cards.how: Train a wide autoencoder on the activations with an L1 penalty: $\mathcal{L} = \|x-\hat x\|^2 + \lambda\|h\|_1$.
cards.when: When you want a list of the features a layer uses.

cards.title: Dead features
cards.what: Some autoencoder units never turn on, so they waste space.
cards.why: They make the feature list look bigger than it is.
cards.how: Count how often each unit fires during training. Re-start the units that never fire.
cards.when: When you train your own sparse autoencoder.

cards.title: Circuit
cards.what: A small group of connected parts inside the model that does one job together.
cards.why: Features tell you what is stored. Circuits tell you how it is used.
cards.how: Trace which heads and neurons pass information to each other, then test the path by patching.
cards.when: When you ask how the model computes an answer.

cards.title: Induction head
cards.what: Two attention heads that work together to copy what came after the last time a token appeared.
cards.why: It is the first circuit found that explains in-context learning.
cards.how: Head 1 marks each token with the token before it. Head 2 looks for a match and copies the next token.
cards.when: When a model repeats patterns from its prompt.

cards.title: Activation patching
cards.what: Swap one part of the network's activations and see what breaks.
cards.why: It tests cause, not just correlation. It fixes the probe trap.
cards.how: Run a clean input and a broken input. Copy one activation from clean to broken. If the output recovers, that part matters.
cards.when: When you want proof that a part matters.

cards.title: Attention as lookup
cards.what: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: a query finds matching keys and takes their values.

cards.title: Habit loop
cards.what: A habit is a cue, then a routine, then a reward. Change the routine, keep the cue.
cards.why: Willpower alone fails. Changing the loop works better.
cards.how: Write down the cue and the reward. Keep them, and swap in a new routine.
cards.when: When you want to stop or start a habit.

cards.title: Deep focus blocks
cards.what: Plan long blocks with no switching. Hard thinking needs time to warm up.
cards.why: Short gaps between meetings are too short for hard work.
cards.how: Block 90 minutes in the calendar. Turn off messages. Do one task only.
cards.when: When you plan a study or coding day.

cards.title: Attention residue
cards.what: After you switch tasks, part of your mind stays on the old task for a while.
cards.why: It explains why checking messages ruins focus even when it is quick.
cards.when: When you decide whether to check your phone.
cards.extra: Not the same as attention in transformers; the merge step kept them apart.
